summary: Algeria requires a consular visa obtained in advance for nearly every nationality — only a handful of Arab and Maghreb states plus a few others are exempt. The main exception is the Saharan tourism scheme, under which tourists booked with an accredited Algerian agency can receive a visa on arrival for the far-southern desert wilayas.

vaccinations.text: A yellow fever vaccination certificate is required for travelers over 1 year of age arriving from countries with risk of yellow fever transmission.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Algeria

travelInsurance.text: Travel insurance covering the whole stay is a standard requirement of the Algerian visa application. Carry proof of cover with your travel documents.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Algeria

onwardTicket.text: Visa applications must normally include a return or onward flight booking, and border officers can ask to see it on arrival.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Algeria

proofOfFunds.text: No fixed amount is published for tourists; consulates may ask for bank statements with the visa application and border officers can ask about your means of support.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Algeria

currencyLimits.text: Foreign currency above roughly EUR 1,000 equivalent should be declared on arrival and the declaration kept. You may need it to take unspent cash out again. Import and export of Algerian dinars is prohibited beyond a small allowance; confirm current thresholds before travel.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Algeria

notes: The Algerian dinar is not convertible abroad — change money inside Algeria, keep exchange receipts and spend or re-exchange dinars before departure.
Drones may not be brought in without prior authorization and are routinely confiscated at the border.

payments.text: Algeria is overwhelmingly cash-based — international cards work only at a handful of upscale hotels and ATMs, so bring euros or dollars to exchange. A parallel exchange market exists but using it is technically illegal.

safety.text: Northern cities such as Algiers, Oran and Constantine are generally safe with normal precautions. Western governments advise against travel near the Libyan, Malian and Nigerien borders and parts of the Sahara — far-south desert tourism is done with accredited agencies, which the visa-on-arrival scheme requires anyway.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Algeria Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: Spring and fall are ideal for the coast and the north; the Sahara season runs roughly October to April, when desert days are mild.

idp.text: Algeria is a party to the 1949 Geneva Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1968 Vienna one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1949 Geneva version. A permit issued under the 1968 Vienna Convention carries no treaty obligation here.

source.name: UN Treaty Collection — Convention on Road Traffic (Geneva, 1949), status of parties
source.instrument: Convention on Road Traffic, Geneva, 19 September 1949 (UNTS vol. 125, p. 3)

driving.text: Algeria is a party to the 1949 Geneva Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1968 Vienna one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1949 Geneva version. A permit issued under the 1968 Vienna Convention carries no treaty obligation here. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Algeria yet.

tips.text: Since 2023, tourists joining an organized tour with an accredited Algerian agency can obtain a visa on arrival for the far-southern Sahara (Djanet, Tamanrasset and nearby wilayas). The agency files the request in advance and meets you at the airport. It is not valid for independent travel or for the north of the country.

For a standard consular visa, Algerian consulates generally require either a certified invitation (certificat d'hébergement) from a host in Algeria or confirmed hotel bookings covering the whole stay.
Plan around cash: exchange euros or dollars at banks or hotels, keep the receipts, and re-exchange leftover dinars before you leave. The dinar cannot be changed abroad.

Avoid areas close to the borders with Libya, Mali, Mauritania and Niger — governments warn of terrorism and kidnapping risk there, and travel in much of the deep Sahara requires escorts arranged through your agency.
Do not photograph government buildings, police, military sites or infrastructure. It can lead to questioning or detention.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Algeria?
faq.answer: Almost certainly yes. Algeria exempts only a short list of mostly Arab and Maghreb nationalities (such as Tunisia, Libya, Morocco, Mauritania, Mali, Malaysia, Seychelles and Syria). Everyone else — including all EU, UK, US, Canadian and Australian citizens — must obtain a visa from an Algerian consulate before travel, unless entering under the Saharan tour visa-on-arrival scheme.

faq.question: Does Algeria have an eVisa?
faq.answer: No. Algeria has no general eVisa; visas are issued by consulates. The only on-arrival option is the Saharan tourism scheme for organized tours to the far south.

faq.question: Can I get an Algerian visa on arrival?
faq.answer: Only under the Saharan tourism scheme introduced in 2023: if you book a tour of the far-southern desert wilayas (for example Djanet or Tamanrasset) with an accredited Algerian agency, the agency arranges a visa issued on arrival at the airport. It cannot be used for independent travel or for northern Algeria.

faq.question: Can I use my credit card in Algeria?
faq.answer: Rarely — only some upscale hotels and a few ATMs accept international cards. Bring cash in euros or dollars, exchange as needed, and keep receipts so you can re-exchange dinars before leaving, as the dinar is not convertible abroad.

faq.question: Can Israeli citizens visit Algeria?
faq.answer: No — Israeli passport holders are not admitted to Algeria.
